rv.q: In his Broadway debut, Enscoe, a member of the indie folk band Bandits on the Run, beautifully conveys how brash, youthful hope can lead to places unimagined, for better and worse.
The songs, by the Avett Brothers, are lovely, but the musical lacks the dramatic architecture to support them effectively.
But it strikes me as a weird, sure, but also daring interpretation of a kind of music we only rarely hear on Broadway.
The new musical 'Swept Away,' featuring songs by the Avett Brothers, offers moments of genuine emotion and beautiful melodies, but struggles to fully coalesce into a dramatically satisfying whole.
But if they've come for a satisfying story, they'll leave hungry.
Ultimately, Swept Away’s most compelling elements exist around its center rather than within it.
The second half of the show is impenetrably strange.
Despite it all, for me, 'Swept Away' does not land.
But it’s tough to escape the feeling that the production and the audience are stranded together until it’s over.

What he proceeds to recount is one of the most harrowing and captivating tales currently on Broadway.
In just one act, “Swept Away” delivers a fresh story and a spiritual journey, both rare assets in contemporary Broadway musicals.
“Swept Away” is an awesomely different and totally unexpected Broadway musical.
Swept Away is an original and adventurous foray along the darker edges of what musical theatre can accomplish.

It’s strong stuff, and hardly the sort of musical for tourists simply looking for a fun time. But this superbly staged and acted production exerts a powerful, hypnotic force that demands attention and respect.
Others are urged to come sail away on this often-remarkable journey.
The musical adaptation of the Avett Brothers' folk-rock catalog feels emotionally authentic, even when the plot occasionally feels forced into the framework of their existing songs.
Rather, it left me aware of the qualities that were in insufficient supply – tension and details and meaning.
The Avett Brothers’ music is glorious, but the show feels too becalmed and dull around their lovely, if repetitive, score.
Maybe they’ll defy the odds — for artistic reasons, I hope they do — but I ultimately expect Swept Away will be pulled out to sea in the next tide.
The new work is obviously a labor of love executed with exemplary taste but, in the end, lacking in qualities by which an audience is likely to be swept away.

Away is professionally staged, the limitations of John Logan’s story and characterization undermine its power and theme, the same fault to be found with his co-writing credit on the book for Sting’s The Last Ship in 2014.
…eventually starts to sink under the weight of its solemnity.
The forces which drive a man to his basest survival instincts would make for compelling theatre but, again, the musical keeps insight at bay.
Swept Away is a riveting odyssey and if you can allow yourself to break free of genre-convention, you’re in for a thought provoking and sublime experience.

Thanks to the solid direction by Tony Michael Mayer, the choreography by David Neumann, the set design by Rachael Huack, the lighting design by Kevin Adams, and the sound design by John Shivers, the onstage shipwreck is as real as one could imagine.
Despite all this effort, Swept Away hasn’t found a rationale for telling its nightmarish story.
Overall, “Swept Away” is a high-adrenaline and pulse-pounding new Broadway musical.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Avett Brothers musical about shipwrecked sailors, praising the gorgeous folk-rock score and strong performances but finding the dark, morality-tale narrative sleepy, underdeveloped, and dramatically uneven.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.vl: Skip for any show with detail
sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
